transcript.text: Good afternoon. In today's lecture, I want to look at how students can improve their memory. Many of you probably think memory is a talent you either have or don't, but research suggests that technique matters far more than talent.
transcript.speaker: DR ELLIS

transcript.text: The German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus was the first person to study forgetting scientifically. He tested himself on lists of meaningless syllables and found that we forget most new information very quickly.
transcript.speaker: DR ELLIS

transcript.text: His results showed that after one day we typically lose about two thirds of what we learnt. The loss is fastest in the first hour, and then it slows down, which is why early review is so valuable.
transcript.speaker: DR ELLIS

transcript.text: This pattern has been confirmed many times since, in different countries and with different kinds of material, so we can treat it as one of the most reliable findings in psychology. The practical message for students is clear: do not leave your revision until the night before an exam.
transcript.speaker: DR ELLIS

transcript.text: The good news is that we can slow this down by reviewing information at the right moments. This is called spaced repetition. For example, you might review a new topic after one day, then after a week, then after a month.
transcript.speaker: DR ELLIS

transcript.text: A second technique is retrieval practice. Instead of simply re-reading your notes, you close the book and try to recall the main points. It feels harder, but experiments show that students who test themselves remember around fifty percent more.
transcript.speaker: DR ELLIS

transcript.text: Many students also like to highlight text with a coloured pen. Unfortunately, studies show that highlighting alone has very little effect. It gives a feeling of progress, but it doesn't involve real thinking.
transcript.speaker: DR ELLIS

transcript.text: I often ask my own students how they revise, and the answers are quite revealing. Most of them say they read through their notes several times, which is exactly the method that research shows to be the least efficient. It feels comfortable, but comfort is not the same as learning.
transcript.speaker: DR ELLIS

transcript.text: Let me move on to some other strategies. The first is sleep. During sleep, the brain organises memories, so studying late at night and then sleeping badly is a poor strategy. Most researchers recommend at least eight hours.
transcript.speaker: DR ELLIS

transcript.text: Second, exercise. A short walk before studying increases blood flow to the brain, and some students find that they concentrate better after twenty minutes of light activity.
transcript.speaker: DR ELLIS

transcript.text: Third, teaching others. If you explain a topic to a friend, you quickly discover which parts you don't really understand. Some students even record short videos of themselves explaining ideas.
transcript.speaker: DR ELLIS

transcript.text: Fourth, the environment. Try to study in the same quiet place every day, because the brain begins to associate that place with concentration. Switch off your phone, or at least put it in another room.
transcript.speaker: DR ELLIS

transcript.text: Finally, make your notes visual. Diagrams and mind maps help many people remember the links between ideas better than long paragraphs of text. A simple drawing can often replace a page of writing.
transcript.speaker: DR ELLIS

transcript.text: None of these methods requires special equipment or a lot of money. What they do require is a change of habit, and that is always the hardest part, so I suggest starting with just one technique and practising it for a few weeks before adding another.
transcript.speaker: DR ELLIS

transcript.text: I hope these ideas are useful. Try one or two this week and see what happens. Thank you.
transcript.speaker: DR ELLIS
